items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “A recurrent failure to resist impulses to steal objects that are not needed for personal use or for their monetary value”?
items.answer: Kleptomania
items.markingKey: Kleptomania: a recurrent failure to resist impulses to steal objects that are not needed for personal use or for their monetary value. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Gambling disorder is classified as a non-substance addictive disorder in DSM-5. Reason (R): It shares features with substance addictions, such as tolerance and withdrawal-like restlessness. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Shared features are why it is grouped with addictions. [1]

items.stem: Describe the characteristics of kleptomania.
items.answer: Repeated failure to resist impulses to steal objects not needed for personal use or their value; rising tension before the theft and pleasure, gratification or relief during it; the stealing is not done out of anger or revenge or because of delusions or hallucinations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark impulse/not needed; 1 mark tension and relief; 1 mark exclusions [3]

items.stem: Tomás, a well-paid accountant in Madrid, has repeatedly taken cheap items such as pens and soap from shops. She feels tense before taking them, relieved afterwards, and later throws the items away. Suggest one treatment that could help Tomás.
items.answer: Covert sensitisation (imagining stealing paired with aversive images such as vomiting) or naltrexone to reduce urges.
items.markingKey: 1 mark treatment; 1 mark how it helps [2]

items.stem: Yusuf, a well-paid accountant in Karachi, has repeatedly taken cheap items such as pens and soap from shops. She feels tense before taking them, relieved afterwards, and later throws the items away. (a) Explain why her behaviour would not be classified as kleptomania if she stole to sell the items. (b) Suggest one treatment that could help Yusuf.
items.answer: (a) Kleptomania excludes theft for monetary gain; stealing for profit would be ordinary theft. (b) Covert sensitisation (imagining stealing paired with aversive images such as vomiting) or naltrexone to reduce urges.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark exclusion; 1 mark explained [2] (b) 1 mark treatment; 1 mark how it helps [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the DSM-5 classification of impulse control and gambling disorders in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about usefulness.
items.answer: Strength (reliability): Specific criteria (for example four of nine gambling criteria in 12 months) help clinicians agree on a diagnosis. Strength (usefulness): Recognising gambling as an addiction encourages treatment rather than only punishment. Weakness (validity): It can be difficult to distinguish kleptomania from ordinary theft, because the diagnosis depends on the person’s own report of their motives. Weakness (labelling): Labelling behaviour such as fire-setting as a disorder may be used to excuse responsibility, which raises legal and ethical issues. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Define the term ‘kleptomania’.
items.answer: A recurrent failure to resist impulses to steal objects that are not needed for personal use or for their monetary value.

items.stem: A student writes: “Most people who shoplift have kleptomania.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Most shoplifting is done for gain or need; kleptomania is rare and involves stealing items not needed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Describe three DSM-5 criteria for gambling disorder.
items.answer: Any three of: needs to gamble with increasing amounts of money to feel excitement; restless or irritable when cutting down; repeated unsuccessful attempts to stop; preoccupied with gambling; gambles when distressed; chases losses; lies to hide gambling; has jeopardised relationships or work; relies on others for money.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each criterion [3]

items.stem: Explain how operant conditioning can explain gambling disorder.
items.answer: Wins act as positive reinforcement; on a variable-ratio schedule they are unpredictable, so behaviour is very resistant to extinction; gambling may also be negatively reinforced by relief from low mood or stress.
items.markingKey: 1 mark positive reinforcement; 1 mark variable ratio; 1 mark negative reinforcement [3]

items.stem: Nadia plays an online slot game in Doha every evening. Nadia says: “I nearly won three times today, so a big win is definitely coming.” Explain why near misses encourage Nadia to keep playing.
items.answer: Near misses activate the reward system and feel like nearly winning, acting as reinforcement and suggesting skill or that a win is close.
items.markingKey: 1 mark reinforcing; 1 mark belief [2]

items.stem: Samuel plays an online slot game in Jakarta every evening. Samuel says: “I nearly won three times today, so a big win is definitely coming.” (a) Identify the cognitive bias shown by Samuel. (b) Explain why near misses encourage Samuel to keep playing.
items.answer: (a) Gambler’s fallacy (and interpreting near misses as nearly winning). (b) Near misses activate the reward system and feel like nearly winning, acting as reinforcement and suggesting skill or that a win is close.

items.stem: Evaluate Griffiths’ (1994) study of cognitive biases in fruit-machine gambling, including a discussion of the thinking aloud method.
items.answer: Strength (qualitative data): Verbalisations gave insight into gamblers’ actual thoughts, such as personifying the machine. Strength (ecological validity): Participants played real fruit machines in a real arcade, so their behaviour was close to normal gambling. Weakness (the thinking aloud method): Speaking thoughts aloud is unnatural and may change how people think while playing. Weakness (generalisability): The sample was small and from one area in the UK, mostly male, so it may not apply to other gamblers. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: A student writes: “A gambler who believes they can predict a slot machine’s results is showing an illusion of control.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.

items.stem: Explain how cognitive biases can maintain gambling.
items.answer: Gamblers may believe they have skill or control (illusion of control), see near misses as nearly winning, or think a win is “due” (gambler’s fallacy), so they continue despite losses.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “A behavioural therapy in which the person imagines the unwanted behaviour paired with an unpleasant consequence”?
items.answer: Covert sensitisation
items.markingKey: Covert sensitisation: a behavioural therapy in which the person imagines the unwanted behaviour paired with an unpleasant consequence. [1]

items.stem: Describe how covert sensitisation could be used to treat kleptomania.
items.answer: The client imagines approaching and stealing an item, then imagines an aversive outcome such as nausea, vomiting or being caught; repeated pairing makes the urge to steal associated with disgust, reducing the behaviour (Glover, 2011, used nausea imagery).
items.markingKey: 1 mark imagined behaviour; 1 mark aversive imagery; 1 mark association reduces urge [3]

items.stem: Describe imaginal desensitisation as a treatment for gambling disorder.
items.answer: The client learns relaxation, then while relaxed imagines scenes that trigger the urge to gamble and imagines leaving without gambling; the urge becomes associated with relaxation and control rather than arousal.
items.markingKey: 1 mark relaxation; 1 mark imagined trigger and resisting; 1 mark mechanism [3]

items.stem: Amara, aged 30, from Dhaka, has set several fires in rubbish bins and feels intense excitement watching them burn. A therapist suggests covert sensitisation. Explain one weakness of this treatment.
items.answer: It may only work if Amara imagines scenes vividly and practises outside sessions, and evidence comes mainly from case studies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark weakness; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Grace, aged 30, from Riyadh, has set several fires in rubbish bins and feels intense excitement watching them burn. A therapist suggests covert sensitisation. (a) Explain one weakness of this treatment. (b) Suggest one other treatment and explain how it might help.
items.answer: (a) It may only work if Grace imagines scenes vividly and practises outside sessions, and evidence comes mainly from case studies. (b) Naltrexone, which may reduce the excitement or urge associated with fire-setting by blocking opioid receptors.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark weakness; 1 mark explained [2] (b) 1 mark treatment; 1 mark mechanism [2]

items.stem: Evaluate imaginal desensitisation as a treatment for gambling disorder, including a discussion of ethics.
items.answer: Strength (ethics): It involves no real punishment or drugs, so it is non-invasive and low risk. Strength (effectiveness): Studies such as McConaghy et al. found imaginal desensitisation reduced gambling more than aversion therapy, with benefits at follow-up. Weakness (individual differences): It relies on clients being able to imagine scenes vividly and practise relaxation, which not everyone can do. Weakness (generalisability): Much of the evidence comes from small samples, so it is uncertain how well it works for all gamblers. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Discuss whether gambling disorder is best explained by behavioural (operant conditioning) factors.
items.answer: Arguments for: Variable-ratio reinforcement on slot machines produces persistent behaviour that resists extinction. Near misses and occasional wins act as reinforcers. Arguments against: Cognitive biases (Griffiths, 1994: regular gamblers made more irrational verbalisations) also maintain gambling. Biochemical factors such as dopamine and opioid reward systems are involved, supported by the effectiveness of naltrexone. Not everyone who is reinforced develops a disorder. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

The percentage of each participant’s verbalisations that were irrational was compared for 6 regular and 6 non-regular gamblers. Table: Irrational verbalisations (%) — Regular gamblers: 10, 16, 10, 15, 12, 14. Non-regular gamblers: 8, 4, 4, 1, 5, 7. (a) Name the experimental design used in this study and explain one weakness of using this design here. (b) The participants were people selected from a full list of residents of Muscat using a random number generator. Identify the sampling technique used and explain one weakness of it.
items.answer: (a) Independent measures: different participants take part in each condition. Weakness: participant variables (individual differences between the two groups) may explain the difference in the DV instead of the IV. (b) Random sampling. Weakness: random selection does not guarantee a representative sample, especially when the sample is small, and some people may refuse.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct design; 1 mark: weakness explained in context [2] (b) 1 mark: sampling technique; 1 mark: weakness explained [2]

items.stem: ‘Psychological treatments are more effective than drug treatments for impulse control disorders.’ Discuss this view. In your answer, you may refer to case studies, effectiveness and generalisability.
items.answer: Arguments for: Imaginal desensitisation and covert sensitisation target the learned urge and teach control. Case studies (for example Glover, 2011) report long-lasting improvement. Arguments against: Naltrexone reduces urges in many patients in controlled trials. Evidence for psychological treatments often comes from small samples or single cases. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “Persistent and recurrent problematic gambling leading to significant impairment or distress”?
items.answer: Gambling disorder
items.markingKey: Gambling disorder: persistent and recurrent problematic gambling leading to significant impairment or distress. [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Describe the characteristics of kleptomania. (b) In a revision session, a student says: “People with gambling disorder may need to gamble with increasing amounts of money to feel excitement.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Repeated failure to resist impulses to steal objects not needed for personal use or their value; rising tension before the theft and pleasure, gratification or relief during it; the stealing is not done out of anger or revenge or because of delusions or hallucinations. (b) Correct. This resembles tolerance in substance addiction.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark impulse/not needed; 1 mark tension and relief; 1 mark exclusions [3] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: The DSM-5 classification of impulse control and gambling disorders can be evaluated in terms of usefulness. Explain one strength of the study relating to this issue.
items.answer: Recognising gambling as an addiction encourages treatment rather than only punishment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to usefulness; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Priya replicated Griffiths’ (1994) “thinking aloud” study in an arcade in Lima. The percentage of each participant’s verbalisations that were irrational was compared for 7 regular and 7 non-regular gamblers. Table: Irrational verbalisations (%) — Regular gamblers: 10, 15, 7, 14, 13, 7, 9. Non-regular gamblers: 1, 4, 0, 4, 0, 2, 4. Identify the independent variable (IV) and the dependent variable (DV) in this study.
items.answer: IV: whether participants were regular or non-regular gamblers. DV: the percentage of each participant’s spoken statements coded as irrational.

items.stem: Ana, a well-paid accountant in Dhaka, has repeatedly taken cheap items such as pens and soap from shops. She feels tense before taking them, relieved afterwards, and later throws the items away. Explain why her behaviour would not be classified as kleptomania if she stole to sell the items.
items.answer: Kleptomania excludes theft for monetary gain; stealing for profit would be ordinary theft.
items.markingKey: 1 mark exclusion; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Tariq, a well-paid accountant in Jakarta, has repeatedly taken cheap items such as pens and soap from shops. She feels tense before taking them, relieved afterwards, and later throws the items away. (a) Explain why her behaviour would not be classified as kleptomania if she stole to sell the items. (b) Suggest one treatment that could help Tariq.
items.answer: (a) Kleptomania excludes theft for monetary gain; stealing for profit would be ordinary theft. (b) Covert sensitisation (imagining stealing paired with aversive images such as vomiting) or naltrexone to reduce urges.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark exclusion; 1 mark explained [2] (b) 1 mark treatment; 1 mark how it helps [2]

items.stem: Design a laboratory experiment to investigate whether near-miss outcomes increase the desire to keep playing a game of chance. Your plan must include: the experimental design, ethical issues, controls and how the dependent variable will be measured.
items.answer: Method: a laboratory experiment. Manipulate the IV in a controlled room; standardised procedure and instructions; measure the DV objectively. Variables: IV: near-miss or clear-loss outcomes; DV: number of extra plays chosen. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Cairo, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “The belief that one can influence outcomes that are actually determined by chance”.
items.answer: Illusion of control
items.markingKey: Illusion of control: the belief that one can influence outcomes that are actually determined by chance. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “Operant conditioning cannot explain why people continue to gamble after losing.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain how operant conditioning can explain gambling disorder.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Variable-ratio reinforcement and near misses explain persistence despite losses. (b) Wins act as positive reinforcement; on a variable-ratio schedule they are unpredictable, so behaviour is very resistant to extinction; gambling may also be negatively reinforced by relief from low mood or stress.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark positive reinforcement; 1 mark variable ratio; 1 mark negative reinforcement [3]

items.stem: With reference to Griffiths’ (1994) study of cognitive biases in fruit-machine gambling, explain one weakness relating to reliability of coding.
items.answer: Deciding whether a statement was irrational involved interpretation, so coders might disagree.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to reliability of coding; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Ana plays an online slot game in Seoul every evening. Ana says: “I nearly won three times today, so a big win is definitely coming.” Use operant conditioning to explain why the game is difficult to stop playing.
items.answer: Wins occur on a variable-ratio schedule, so behaviour is highly resistant to extinction; each unpredictable win reinforces playing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark VR schedule; 1 mark resistance to extinction [2]

items.stem: ‘Gambling disorder is best explained by behavioural (operant conditioning) factors.’ To what extent do you agree? In your answer, you may refer to biochemical explanations, cognitive biases and individual differences.
items.answer: Arguments for: Variable-ratio reinforcement on slot machines produces persistent behaviour that resists extinction. Near misses and occasional wins act as reinforcers. Arguments against: Cognitive biases (Griffiths, 1994: regular gamblers made more irrational verbalisations) also maintain gambling. Biochemical factors such as dopamine and opioid reward systems are involved, supported by the effectiveness of naltrexone. Not everyone who is reinforced develops a disorder. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: What is meant by ‘imaginal desensitisation’?
items.answer: A therapy in which a relaxed person imagines a situation that triggers the urge and imagines resisting it.
items.markingKey: Imaginal desensitisation: a therapy in which a relaxed person imagines a situation that triggers the urge and imagines resisting it. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: Arjun, aged 30, from Lagos, has set several fires in rubbish bins and feels intense excitement watching them burn. A therapist suggests covert sensitisation. (a) Describe how covert sensitisation would be used with Arjun. (b) Explain one weakness of this treatment.
items.answer: (a) Arjun imagines preparing to set a fire, then imagines unpleasant consequences such as choking on smoke, severe burns or being arrested, until the urge is linked with these images. (b) It may only work if Arjun imagines scenes vividly and practises outside sessions, and evidence comes mainly from case studies.
